title: General Surgery Diploma — Upper Limb: Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics MCQ Bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which structures pierce the clavipectoral fascia (costocoracoid membrane) between the clavicle and pectoralis minor?
options: Cephalic vein, thoracoacromial artery, lateral pectoral nerve, and lymphatic vessels
Basilic vein, medial pectoral nerve, and ulnar nerve
Axillary artery, axillary vein, and radial nerve
Long thoracic nerve and thoracodorsal nerve
questions.explanation: Four structures pierce the clavipectoral fascia: cephalic vein, thoracoacromial artery (and vein), lateral pectoral nerve, and lymphatics passing to apical axillary nodes.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: From which cervical fascia layer is the axillary sheath derived, and what structures does it enclose?
options: Investing layer; encloses axillary vein and long thoracic nerve
Prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia; encloses the axillary artery and cords of the brachial plexus (plus axillary vein per Snell)
Pretracheal fascia; encloses subclavian vein only
Superficial fascia; encloses cephalic vein
questions.explanation: The axillary sheath is a tubular prolongation of the prevertebral fascia extending from the neck into the axilla around the axillary artery and brachial plexus cords.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which artery provides the primary blood supply (~60%) to the lateral part of the female breast?
options: Internal thoracic (mammary) artery
Lateral thoracic artery (branch of 2nd part of axillary artery)
Posterior intercostal arteries
Subscapular artery
questions.explanation: The lateral thoracic artery supplies approximately 60% of the breast (mainly lateral quadrants) via lateral mammary branches, while perforators of the internal thoracic artery supply the medial part.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Where does lymph from the lateral quadrants of the breast primarily drain initially?
options: Apical axillary lymph nodes directly
Anterior (pectoral) group of axillary lymph nodes
Parasternal (internal thoracic) lymph nodes
Subphrenic plexus
questions.explanation: Approximately 75% of breast lymph—especially from the lateral quadrants and nipple/areola—drains first into the anterior (pectoral) axillary nodes located along the lower border of pectoralis minor.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Where does lymph from the lower medial quadrant of the breast have a potential pathway to spread, risking hepatic or pelvic metastasis?
options: Lateral axillary nodes
Lymphatic plexus of the rectus sheath and subphrenic peritoneal plexus
Supratrochlear lymph nodes
Deltopectoral (infraclavicular) nodes
questions.explanation: Lymphatics from the inferomedial breast communicate through the upper anterior abdominal wall with the subperitoneal/subphrenic plexus, allowing transcoelomic spread (e.g., Krukenberg tumor).
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which superficial vein ascends in the deltopectoral groove between the deltoid and pectoralis major muscles?
options: Basilic vein
Cephalic vein
Median cubital vein
Brachial vein
questions.explanation: The cephalic vein arises from the lateral end of the dorsal venous arch, ascends along the lateral arm, runs in the deltopectoral groove, and pierces the clavipectoral fascia to enter the axillary vein.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Where does the basilic vein pierce the deep fascia of the arm to join the venae comitantes of the brachial artery and form the axillary vein?
options: In the deltopectoral groove
At the middle of the medial side of the arm (basilic hiatus), continuing as the axillary vein at the lower border of teres major
At the wrist
At the lateral border of the first rib
questions.explanation: The basilic vein pierces the deep fascia near the mid-arm, accompanies the brachial artery, and unites with the venae comitantes at the lower border of teres major to form the axillary vein.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which anatomical structure lies immediately deep to the median cubital vein in the cubital fossa, protecting the underlying brachial artery during venipuncture?
options: Pronator teres muscle
Bicipital aponeurosis (lacertus fibrosus)
Brachioradialis tendon
Flexor retinaculum
questions.explanation: The bicipital aponeurosis separates the superficial median cubital vein from the deeper brachial artery and median nerve, preventing accidental intra-arterial injection.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Where are the supratrochlear (epitrochlear) lymph nodes located, and which region do they drain?
options: In the deltopectoral groove; drain the lateral hand and forearm
Just above the medial epicondyle (in front of trochlea); receive lymph from the medial side of the hand and forearm
In the cubital fossa; drain the shoulder joint
Posterior to the acromion; drain the scapular skin
questions.explanation: Supratrochlear nodes lie in superficial fascia above the medial epicondyle along the basilic vein and drain the medial (ulnar) hand and forearm before sending efferents to the lateral axillary nodes.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Where are the infraclavicular (deltopectoral) lymph nodes located, and which territory do they drain?
options: Along the subscapular vessels; drain the back
In the deltopectoral groove below the clavicle along the cephalic vein; drain the lateral side of the hand, forearm, and arm
Deep to pectoralis minor; drain the medial breast
Along the axillary vein; drain the anterior abdominal wall
questions.explanation: Deltopectoral nodes accompany the cephalic vein from the radial side of the limb and send efferent vessels through the clavipectoral fascia directly to the apical axillary lymph nodes.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which axillary lymph node group receives efferents from all other axillary lymph node groups and drains via the subclavian lymph trunk?
options: Anterior (pectoral) group
Posterior (subscapular) group
Central group
Apical group
questions.explanation: The apical group lies at the apex of the axilla medial to the 1st part of the axillary vein; it receives lymph from the central, anterior, posterior, lateral, and infraclavicular nodes and forms the subclavian lymph trunk.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: What are the anatomical boundaries of the quadrangular space in the posterior scapular/axillary region?
options: Superiorly: teres minor; Inferiorly: teres major; Medially: long head of triceps; Laterally: surgical neck of humerus
Superiorly: teres major; Inferiorly: latissimus dorsi; Medially: medial border of scapula; Laterally: humerus
Superiorly: supraspinatus; Inferiorly: infraspinatus; Medially: spine of scapula; Laterally: acromion
Superiorly: clavicle; Inferiorly: first rib; Medially: scalenus anterior; Laterally: coracoid process
questions.explanation: The quadrangular space is bounded above by teres minor (and subscapularis), below by teres major, medially by the long head of triceps, and laterally by the surgical neck of the humerus.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which neurovascular structures pass through the quadrangular space?
options: Radial nerve and profunda brachii artery
Axillary (circumflex) nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery and vein
Circumflex scapular artery
Suprascapular nerve and artery
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels traverse the quadrangular space closely applied to the surgical neck of the humerus and inferior capsule of the shoulder joint.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which structure passes through the upper triangular space (bounded by teres minor, teres major, and long head of triceps)?
options: Radial nerve
Circumflex scapular artery
Axillary nerve
Thoracodorsal nerve
questions.explanation: The circumflex scapular branch of the subscapular artery passes posteriorly through the upper triangular space to enter the infraspinous fossa and join the scapular anastomosis.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which structures pass through the lower triangular space (triangular interval) below teres major, lateral to the long head of triceps, and medial to the humerus?
options: Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery
Radial nerve and profunda brachii artery
Ulnar nerve and superior ulnar collateral artery
Median nerve and brachial artery
questions.explanation: The radial nerve and profunda brachii vessels exit the axilla inferiorly through the triangular interval to enter the spiral (radial) groove on the posterior humerus.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: In the suprascapular notch, what is the anatomical relationship of the suprascapular artery and nerve to the superior transverse scapular ligament?
options: Both pass beneath the ligament
Both pass above the ligament
The suprascapular artery passes ABOVE the ligament, while the suprascapular nerve passes UNDER (through the notch beneath) the ligament
The nerve passes above and the artery passes under
questions.explanation: Classic anatomical rule ('Army over the bridge, Navy under the bridge'): the suprascapular artery runs above the transverse scapular ligament, whereas the suprascapular nerve passes through the foramen underneath it.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which nerve supplies the skin of the upper medial aspect of the arm and floor of the axilla, and is NOT a branch of the brachial plexus?
options: Medial brachial cutaneous nerve
Intercostobrachial nerve (lateral cutaneous branch of 2nd intercostal nerve, T2)
Supraclavicular nerve
Axillary nerve
questions.explanation: The intercostobrachial nerve (T2) crosses the axilla to supply the skin of the upper medial arm; it is frequently encountered (and preserved if possible) during axillary lymph node clearance.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which nerve supplies the skin over the shoulder cap (upper half of deltoid) and is derived from the cervical plexus rather than the brachial plexus?
options: Upper lateral cutaneous nerve of arm
Supraclavicular nerves (C3, C4)
Dorsal scapular nerve
Long thoracic nerve
questions.explanation: All skin of the upper limb is supplied by the brachial plexus EXCEPT the skin over the shoulder tip (supraclavicular nerves, C3–C4) and the upper medial arm (intercostobrachial nerve, T2).
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which muscle of the upper limb girdle is innervated by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) rather than the brachial plexus?
options: Latissimus dorsi
Trapezius
Rhomboid major
Levator scapulae
questions.explanation: Every muscle acting on the upper limb is supplied by the brachial plexus EXCEPT the trapezius, which receives motor innervation from the spinal part of the accessory nerve (CN XI).
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: How does the axillary vein lie relative to the axillary artery throughout the axilla, and what separates them distally?
options: Lateral to the artery; separated by lateral cord
Medial to the artery; separated from it by the medial cord of the brachial plexus, ulnar nerve, and medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm
Posterior to the artery; separated by posterior cord
Anterior to the artery; separated by pectoralis minor
questions.explanation: The axillary vein lies medial to the axillary artery; between them run the medial cord, ulnar nerve, and medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Where does the axillary artery begin and where does it end?
options: Begins at the lateral border of the 1st rib (as continuation of subclavian artery) and ends at the lower border of teres major (becoming brachial artery)
Begins at the sternoclavicular joint and ends at the cubital fossa
Begins at the medial border of scalenus anterior and ends at pectoralis minor
Begins at the lower border of teres major and ends at the neck of the radius
questions.explanation: The axillary artery extends from the outer border of the 1st rib to the lower border of teres major, divided into three parts by the pectoralis minor muscle.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which branch arises from the FIRST part of the axillary artery (proximal to pectoralis minor)?
options: Thoracoacromial artery
Highest (superior) thoracic artery
Lateral thoracic artery
Subscapular artery
questions.explanation: The 1st part of the axillary artery gives off 1 branch (superior thoracic), the 2nd part gives 2 branches (thoracoacromial and lateral thoracic), and the 3rd part gives 3 branches (subscapular, anterior & posterior circumflex humeral).
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: What are the four terminal branches of the thoracoacromial artery (from the 2nd part of the axillary artery)?
options: Acromial, pectoral, clavicular, and deltoid branches
Suprascapular, dorsal scapular, subscapular, and circumflex scapular
Superior, middle, and inferior ulnar collateral and profunda brachii
Anterior, posterior, medial, and lateral thoracic branches
questions.explanation: The thoracoacromial trunk pierces the clavipectoral fascia and immediately divides into four branches: pectoral, acromial, clavicular, and deltoid (mnemonic: 'ABCD' / 'Cadavers Are Dead People').
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: What is the largest branch of the axillary artery, arising from its 3rd part?
options: Thoracoacromial artery
Subscapular artery (which divides into circumflex scapular and thoracodorsal arteries)
Posterior circumflex humeral artery
Superior thoracic artery
questions.explanation: The subscapular artery is the largest branch of the axillary artery; it descends along the posterior axillary wall, gives off the circumflex scapular artery, and continues as the thoracodorsal artery to latissimus dorsi.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which nerve runs directly posterior to the 1st part of the axillary artery and lies on the superficial surface of serratus anterior?
options: Thoracodorsal nerve
Long thoracic nerve of Bell (C5, C6, C7)
Medial pectoral nerve
Axillary nerve
questions.explanation: The long thoracic nerve (C5–C7) descends behind the 1st part of the axillary artery onto the external surface of serratus anterior.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which arteries participate in the arterial anastomosis around the scapula (providing collateral circulation if the 3rd part of subclavian or 1st part of axillary artery is ligated)?
options: Suprascapular artery & deep branch of transverse cervical (dorsal scapular) artery (from subclavian) anastomosing with subscapular & circumflex scapular arteries (from 3rd part of axillary)
Anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries only
Superior and inferior ulnar collateral arteries
Internal thoracic and superior epigastric arteries
questions.explanation: The scapular anastomosis links the 1st part of the subclavian artery (via thyrocervical trunk: suprascapular & dorsal scapular) with the 3rd part of the axillary artery (via subscapular & circumflex scapular), bypassing occlusion between them.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Why must surgical ligation of the axillary artery NEVER be performed distal to the origin of the subscapular artery (3rd part) unless absolutely unavoidable?
options: Because the scapular collateral anastomosis bypasses proximal segments, whereas distal to the subscapular artery collateral flow to the arm is severely limited
Because it causes immediate necrosis of the clavicle
Because it severs the phrenic nerve
Because the brachial vein drains into it
questions.explanation: The rich scapular anastomosis connects proximal subclavian branches to the subscapular artery; occlusion distal to the subscapular artery compromises perfusion of the upper limb.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Where are the roots and trunks of the brachial plexus anatomically located?
options: Inside the axilla behind pectoralis minor
In the posterior triangle of the neck (emerging between scalenus anterior and scalenus medius)
In the cubital fossa
In the spiral groove of the humerus
questions.explanation: The roots (C5–T1 ventral rami) and trunks (upper, middle, lower) lie in the posterior triangle of the neck; the divisions pass behind the clavicle, and the cords lie in the axilla.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: From which specific components of the brachial plexus does the long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7) arise?
options: Upper trunk
Directly from the roots (C5, C6, C7)
Lateral cord
Posterior cord
questions.explanation: Both the dorsal scapular nerve (C5) and the long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7) arise directly from the roots of the brachial plexus in the neck.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Injury to the long thoracic nerve during radical mastectomy or axillary lymph node dissection causes paralysis of serratus anterior, resulting in:
options: Wrist drop
Winging of the scapula (medial border protrudes posteriorly, especially when pushing against a wall) and inability to abduct the arm above 90 degrees
Claw hand
Loss of elbow flexion
questions.explanation: Serratus anterior holds the medial border of the scapula against the thoracic wall and rotates the glenoid upward for overhead abduction (>90°).
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which two nerves arise from the UPPER trunk (C5, C6) of the brachial plexus?
options: Long thoracic nerve and dorsal scapular nerve
Suprascapular nerve and nerve to subclavius
Lateral pectoral nerve and musculocutaneous nerve
Thoracodorsal nerve and axillary nerve
questions.explanation: The upper trunk is the only trunk that gives off branches: the suprascapular nerve (to supraspinatus and infraspinatus) and the nerve to subclavius.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Traction injury to the upper trunk of the brachial plexus (C5, C6—Erb-Duchenne palsy) produces the classic 'waiter's tip' deformity characterized by:
options: Adducted, medially rotated arm; extended, pronated forearm
Abducted, laterally rotated arm with flexed elbow
Hyperextension of MCP joints and flexion of IP joints
Wrist drop and loss of thumb opposition
questions.explanation: C5–C6 loss paralyzes abductors/lateral rotators (deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor) and elbow flexors/supinators (biceps, brachialis, brachioradialis, supinator), leaving the limb adducted, internally rotated, extended, and pronated.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Hyperabduction injury to the lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8, T1—Klumpke's paralysis) causes:
options: Waiter's tip posture

Complete claw hand (paralysis of all intrinsic hand muscles—lumbricals and interossei) with sensory loss along the medial forearm and hand, plus possible Horner's syndrome (if T1 sympathetic fibers are torn)
Loss of shoulder abduction
Isolated loss of thumb abduction
questions.explanation: C8–T1 supplies all small muscles of the hand via the ulnar and median nerves; avulsion of T1 also disrupts preganglionic sympathetic fibers, causing ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis (Horner's syndrome).
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which branches arise from the POSTERIOR cord of the brachial plexus (Mnemonic: 'ULTRA')?
options: Upper subscapular, Lower subscapular, Thoracodorsal, Radial, and Axillary nerves
Lateral pectoral, Musculocutaneous, and Lateral root of median nerve
Medial pectoral, Ulnar, Medial brachial cutaneous, and Medial antebrachial cutaneous
Suprascapular, Dorsal scapular, and Long thoracic nerves
questions.explanation: The posterior cord (formed by posterior divisions of all three trunks) gives rise to: Upper subscapular, Lower subscapular, Thoracodorsal, Radial, and Axillary nerves.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which nerve supplies latissimus dorsi and accompanies the subscapular/thoracodorsal vessels along the posterior axillary wall?
options: Long thoracic nerve
Thoracodorsal nerve (middle subscapular nerve, C6, C7, C8)
Dorsal scapular nerve
Axillary nerve
questions.explanation: The thoracodorsal nerve arises from the posterior cord and enters the deep surface of latissimus dorsi; it must be identified and preserved during axillary lymphadenectomy.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus or inferior dislocation of the glenohumeral joint most commonly injures which nerve?
options: Radial nerve
Axillary (circumflex) nerve (C5, C6)
Ulnar nerve
Musculocutaneous nerve
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve winds closely around the surgical neck of the humerus; its injury paralyzes deltoid (flattening the shoulder contour and impairing abduction beyond 15°) and teres minor, with sensory loss over the 'regimental badge' area.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which structure forms the Lateral root and Medial root of the median nerve?
options: Lateral root from lateral cord (C5, C6, C7) and Medial root from medial cord (C8, T1)
Lateral root from posterior cord and Medial root from upper trunk
Both roots arise from the medial cord
Lateral root from C5 and Medial root from T1 only
questions.explanation: The median nerve (C5–T1) is formed anterior to the 3rd part of the axillary artery by the union of the lateral root (from lateral cord) and medial root (from medial cord).
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which muscles are supplied by the lateral pectoral nerve vs. the medial pectoral nerve?
options: Lateral pectoral (from lateral cord) supplies pectoralis major; Medial pectoral (from medial cord) pierces and supplies pectoralis minor and the lower sternocostal part of pectoralis major
Lateral pectoral supplies subclavius; Medial pectoral supplies serratus anterior
Both supply only pectoralis minor
Lateral pectoral supplies deltoid; Medial pectoral supplies latissimus dorsi
questions.explanation: The lateral pectoral nerve supplies pectoralis major, whereas the medial pectoral nerve pierces pectoralis minor (innervating it) to reach pectoralis major.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which nerve pierces the coracobrachialis muscle and continues into the forearm as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm?
options: Median nerve
Musculocutaneous nerve (C5, C6, C7)
Radial nerve
Ulnar nerve
questions.explanation: Arising from the lateral cord, the musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis, descends between biceps brachii and brachialis (supplying all three anterior arm muscles: 'BBC'), and terminates as the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: What is the relationship of the cords of the brachial plexus to the SECOND part of the axillary artery (deep to pectoralis minor)?
options: All three cords lie lateral to the artery
They are named strictly according to their anatomical position around the 2nd part: Lateral cord is lateral, Medial cord is medial, and Posterior cord is posterior
All three cords lie anterior to the artery
Only the posterior cord is present
questions.explanation: The cords of the brachial plexus are named after their exact relationship to the 2nd part of the axillary artery behind pectoralis minor.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which structures perforate the medial intermuscular septum in the middle of the arm?
options: Radial nerve and profunda brachii artery
Ulnar nerve, superior ulnar collateral artery, and posterior branch of inferior ulnar collateral artery
Median nerve and brachial artery
Musculocutaneous nerve and cephalic vein
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve descends medial to the brachial artery in the upper arm, then pierces the medial intermuscular septum (accompanied by the superior ulnar collateral vessels) to enter the posterior compartment and pass behind the medial epicondyle.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which structures perforate the lateral intermuscular septum of the arm to enter the anterior compartment above the lateral epicondyle?
options: Ulnar nerve and basilic vein
Radial nerve and anterior descending (radial collateral) branch of profunda brachii artery
Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery
Median nerve and inferior ulnar collateral artery
questions.explanation: After traversing the spiral groove posteriorly, the radial nerve and radial collateral artery pierce the lateral intermuscular septum to lie between brachialis and brachioradialis anteriorly.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: How does the median nerve cross the brachial artery in the middle of the arm?
options: Passes posterior to the artery from medial to lateral
Crosses anterior (superficial) to the brachial artery from lateral to medial
Remains strictly lateral to the artery throughout the arm
Pierces the biceps brachii muscle
questions.explanation: In the upper arm, the median nerve lies lateral to the brachial artery; at the mid-arm (insertion of coracobrachialis), it crosses anteriorly from lateral to medial, lying medial to the artery in the cubital fossa.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Mid-shaft fracture of the humerus (involving the spiral groove) typically injures which nerve and artery?
options: Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery
Radial nerve and profunda brachii (deep brachial) artery
Ulnar nerve and superior ulnar collateral artery
Median nerve and brachial artery
questions.explanation: The radial nerve and profunda brachii artery lie directly against the bone in the spiral groove; mid-shaft humeral fracture causes wrist drop (loss of wrist/finger extension) and sensory loss over the dorsal 1st web space, while sparing triceps (whose branches arise higher).
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Fracture of the medial epicondyle of the humerus directly endangers which nerve?
options: Median nerve
Ulnar nerve (lying in the groove behind the medial epicondyle)
Radial nerve
Musculocutaneous nerve
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve is subcutaneous behind the medial epicondyle ('funny bone') before entering the forearm between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Supracondylar fracture of the humerus in a child places which artery and nerve at immediate risk of laceration or entrapment?
options: Ulnar artery and ulnar nerve
Brachial artery and median nerve (particularly the anterior interosseous branch)
Radial artery and axillary nerve
Profunda brachii artery and musculocutaneous nerve
questions.explanation: Posterior displacement of the distal humeral fragment in a supracondylar fracture can injure the brachial artery (risking Volkmann's ischemic contracture) and the median nerve.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: What is the exact order of contents inside the cubital fossa from LATERAL to MEDIAL ('MBBR' / 'Really Need Beer To Be At My Nicest')?
options: Median nerve → Brachial artery → Biceps tendon → Radial nerve
Radial nerve (under brachioradialis) → Biceps brachii tendon → Brachial artery → Median nerve
Ulnar nerve → Brachial artery → Median nerve → Biceps tendon
Biceps tendon → Radial nerve → Median nerve → Brachial artery
questions.explanation: From lateral to medial within the cubital fossa: Radial nerve (deep to brachioradialis), Biceps tendon, Brachial artery, and Median nerve.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: At what anatomical level does the brachial artery terminate by dividing into the radial and ulnar arteries?
options: At the lower border of teres major
In the cubital fossa at the level of the neck of the radius
Behind the medial epicondyle
At the flexor retinaculum of the wrist
questions.explanation: The brachial artery bifurcates into the radial and ulnar arteries opposite the neck of the radius in the distal cubital fossa.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which arteries form the arterial anastomosis IN FRONT OF the medial epicondyle of the humerus?
options: Anterior branch of inferior ulnar collateral artery (from brachial) + Anterior ulnar recurrent artery (from ulnar)
Superior ulnar collateral artery + Posterior ulnar recurrent artery
Radial collateral artery + Radial recurrent artery
Middle collateral artery + Interosseous recurrent artery
questions.explanation: Anterior to the medial epicondyle, the anterior branch of the inferior ulnar collateral artery anastomoses with the anterior ulnar recurrent artery.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which arteries form the arterial anastomosis BEHIND the medial epicondyle of the humerus?
options: Superior ulnar collateral artery + Posterior branch of inferior ulnar collateral artery + Posterior ulnar recurrent artery
Radial collateral artery + Radial recurrent artery
Anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries
Anterior interosseous and palmar carpal arteries
questions.explanation: Behind the medial epicondyle, the superior ulnar collateral and posterior branch of inferior ulnar collateral anastomose with the posterior ulnar recurrent artery.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which arteries form the arterial anastomosis IN FRONT OF and BEHIND the lateral epicondyle of the humerus?
options: In front: Radial collateral (anterior descending branch of profunda brachii) + Radial recurrent artery; Behind: Middle collateral (posterior descending branch of profunda brachii) + Interosseous recurrent artery
Superior and inferior ulnar collateral arteries
Suprascapular and circumflex scapular arteries
Princeps pollicis and radialis indicis arteries
questions.explanation: Around the lateral epicondyle, the two descending terminal branches of profunda brachii anastomose anteriorly with the radial recurrent artery and posteriorly with the interosseous recurrent artery.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: How many muscular branches does the ulnar nerve give off in the arm?
options: Supplies biceps and brachialis
Supplies medial head of triceps
Zero (gives off no muscular branches in the arm, only an articular branch to the elbow joint)
Supplies coracobrachialis
questions.explanation: Neither the median nerve nor the ulnar nerve supplies any muscles in the arm (except the median nerve occasionally giving a twig to pronator teres just above the elbow).
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which muscle in the anterior compartment of the arm is innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve AND assists in flexing and adducting the shoulder joint?
options: Brachialis
Coracobrachialis
Biceps brachii
Anconeus
questions.explanation: Coracobrachialis is pierced and innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve and acts solely on the shoulder joint (flexion and weak adduction).
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: What is the primary action of the biceps brachii muscle when the elbow is flexed to 90 degrees?
options: Pure extension of the elbow
Powerful supination of the forearm (in addition to elbow flexion)
Pronation of the forearm
Adduction of the wrist
questions.explanation: Biceps brachii is the most powerful supinator of the flexed forearm (e.g., driving a screw), whereas supinator acts best when the elbow is extended.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which muscle of the anterior arm is the primary pure flexor of the elbow joint regardless of whether the forearm is pronated or supinated?
options: Biceps brachii
Brachialis
Coracobrachialis
Pronator teres
questions.explanation: Brachialis inserts onto the tuberosity of the ulna (which cannot rotate), making it the pure workhorse flexor of the elbow in all forearm positions.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which muscle of the posterior compartment of the arm is innervated by the radial nerve in the spiral groove and helps stabilize the elbow joint?
options: Anconeus
Supinator
Brachioradialis
Teres minor
questions.explanation: Anconeus is supplied by the branch of the radial nerve to the medial head of triceps within the spiral groove.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Where does the nutrient artery of the humerus enter the bone?
options: At the surgical neck
Near the insertion of coracobrachialis on the medial aspect of the mid-shaft (directed downward toward the elbow)
At the olecranon fossa
At the greater tubercle
questions.explanation: The nutrient artery arises from the brachial artery and enters the humerus near the coracobrachialis insertion, running distally toward the elbow ('to the elbow I go, from the knee I flee').
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which muscle forms the medial boundary of the cubital fossa?
options: Brachioradialis
Pronator teres (lateral border)
Flexor carpi ulnaris
Supinator
questions.explanation: The cubital fossa is bounded laterally by the medial border of brachioradialis, medially by the lateral border of pronator teres, and superiorly by an imaginary line between the humeral epicondyles.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which structures pass THROUGH the carpal tunnel deep to the flexor retinaculum at the wrist?
options: Median nerve, 4 tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis, 4 tendons of flexor digitorum profundus, and tendon of flexor pollicis longus (9 tendons + 1 nerve)
Ulnar nerve, ulnar artery, and median nerve
Radial artery, flexor carpi radialis, and median nerve
Palmaris longus tendon and superficial radial nerve
questions.explanation: Ten structures traverse the carpal tunnel: the median nerve plus 9 flexor tendons (4 FDS, 4 FDP, and 1 FPL). The ulnar nerve/artery pass superficially through Guyon's canal.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Why is cutaneous sensation over the central palm (thenar eminence/hollow of palm) SPARED in carpal tunnel syndrome?
options: Because the ulnar nerve supplies the central palm
Because the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises proximal to the flexor retinaculum and passes superficial to it
Because the radial nerve supplies the palm
Because the palmar cutaneous branch enters Guyon's canal
questions.explanation: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve branches off in the distal forearm and runs above the flexor retinaculum, escaping compression inside the carpal tunnel.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which intrinsic hand muscles are innervated by the recurrent branch of the median nerve and the digital branches of the median nerve (Mnemonic: 'LOAF')?
options: Lateral two lumbricals, Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, and Flexor pollicis brevis (superficial head)
All palmar and dorsal interossei and adductor pollicis
Medial two lumbricals and hypothenar muscles
Palmaris brevis and extensor pollicis brevis
questions.explanation: The median nerve supplies the 'LOAF' muscles in the hand; all other intrinsic hand muscles (hypothenar, interossei, adductor pollicis, medial 2 lumbricals) are supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: What is the cutaneous sensory territory of the median nerve on the palmar and dorsal aspects of the hand?
options: Palmar surface of the lateral 3½ digits (thumb, index, middle, lateral half of ring) and the nail beds (dorsal distal phalanges) of those same 3½ digits
Medial 1½ digits on both palmar and dorsal surfaces
Entire dorsum of the hand
Only the dorsal 1st web space
questions.explanation: The median nerve supplies the palmar skin of the lateral 3½ fingers and wraps around to supply the dorsal skin over their distal phalanges.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which muscles in the anterior compartment of the forearm are NOT innervated by the median nerve (or its anterior interosseous branch)?
options: Flexor digitorum superficialis and pronator teres
Flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus (to ring and little fingers)—both supplied by the ulnar nerve
Flexor pollicis longus and pronator quadratus
Flexor carpi radialis and palmaris longus
questions.explanation: Every muscle in the anterior forearm is supplied by the median nerve EXCEPT flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus, which are innervated by the ulnar nerve.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: What clinical deformity results from a high median nerve lesion at the elbow when the patient attempts to make a fist?
options: Ulnar claw hand
'Hand of benediction' (Pope's blessing)—index and middle fingers remain extended due to paralysis of FDS, lateral half of FDP, and lateral 2 lumbricals, while ring and little fingers flex normally
Wrist drop
Waiter's tip
questions.explanation: In a high median nerve lesion, loss of FDS and the lateral half of FDP prevents flexion of the index and middle fingers during fist formation ('hand of benediction'), alongside ape-hand thumb deformity.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: How does the ulnar nerve enter the hand at the wrist?
options: Deep to the flexor retinaculum inside the carpal tunnel
Superficial to the flexor retinaculum (lateral to the pisiform bone and medial to the ulnar artery) within Guyon's canal
Through the anatomical snuffbox
Behind the styloid process of the radius
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve and ulnar artery pass superficial to the flexor retinaculum in Guyon's canal, radial to the pisiform bone and ulnar to the hook of the hamate.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Explain the 'Ulnar Paradox': why is clawing of the ring and little fingers MORE severe in a distal ulnar nerve lesion at the wrist than in a high lesion at the elbow?
options: Because the radial nerve compensates in a high lesion

Because in a low wrist lesion, the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus (in the forearm) remains intact and actively pulls the DIP joints of the 4th and 5th fingers into unopposed flexion, whereas in a high elbow lesion FDP is paralyzed
Because the median nerve innervates the interossei in high lesions
Because the palmar cutaneous branch is spared at the elbow
questions.explanation: Intact FDP tendons in a distal ulnar nerve injury pull the IP joints into marked flexion while MCP joints hyperextend (unopposed extensors + paralyzed lumbricals/interossei), worsening the claw deformity.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: What does a positive Froment's sign (flexion of the thumb IP joint when trying to pinch a piece of paper) indicate?
options: Median nerve palsy
Ulnar nerve palsy (weakness/paralysis of adductor pollicis, causing the patient to compensate using flexor pollicis longus innervated by the anterior interosseous/median nerve)
Radial nerve palsy
Axillary nerve palsy
questions.explanation: Froment's sign tests adductor pollicis (deep branch of ulnar nerve); when weak, the patient substitutes thumb flexion via FPL (median nerve).
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which muscle in the hand is responsible for abduction of the fingers ('DAB'—Dorsal Interossei Abduct) and is innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve?
options: Palmar interossei
Dorsal interossei (4 bipennate muscles)
Lumbricals
Thenar muscles
questions.explanation: Dorsal interossei abduct the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th digits away from the axial line of the middle finger; palmar interossei adduct them ('PAD'). All interossei are supplied by the deep ulnar nerve.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Injury to the deep branch of the radial nerve (posterior interosseous nerve) at the neck of the radius (e.g., Monteggia fracture) causes:
options: Wrist drop and complete sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand
Finger drop (loss of MCP extension of fingers and thumb extension) WITHOUT wrist drop (extensor carpi radialis longus is spared) and NO sensory loss
Claw hand
Loss of elbow flexion
questions.explanation: Because extensor carpi radialis longus is innervated proximal to the bifurcation of the radial nerve, wrist extension (with radial deviation) is preserved, and the posterior interosseous nerve is purely motor.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which tendons form the boundaries of the anatomical snuffbox on the posterolateral wrist?
options: Anteriorly (laterally): Abductor pollicis longus and Extensor pollicis brevis; Posteriorly (medially): Extensor pollicis longus
Flexor carpi radialis and palmaris longus
Extensor digitorum and extensor indicis
Brachioradialis and pronator teres
questions.explanation: The anatomical snuffbox is bounded laterally by APL and EPB tendons, medially by the EPL tendon, with the scaphoid and trapezium forming its floor.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which structures pass through the anatomical snuffbox?
options: Radial artery (on the floor over scaphoid/trapezium), superficial branch of radial nerve (in roof), and cephalic vein (in roof)
Ulnar artery and ulnar nerve
Median nerve and flexor pollicis longus
Anterior interosseous artery
questions.explanation: The radial artery crosses the floor of the anatomical snuffbox over the scaphoid to enter the 1st dorsal interosseous space, while the cephalic vein and superficial radial nerve cross its roof.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: From which artery is the superficial palmar arch primarily formed, and which branch completes it laterally?
options: Primarily formed by the direct continuation of the ULNAR artery, completed laterally by the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery
Primarily formed by the radial artery, completed by the anterior interosseous artery
Formed equally by superior and inferior ulnar collateral arteries
Formed by the dorsal carpal arch
questions.explanation: The superficial palmar arch lies just deep to the palmar aponeurosis (at the level of the fully extended thumb's distal border) and is mainly derived from the ulnar artery.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: From which artery is the deep palmar arch primarily formed, and which branch completes it medially?
options: Primarily formed by the terminal part of the RADIAL artery (entering via the 1st dorsal interosseous space), completed medially by the deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery
Primarily formed by the ulnar artery
Formed by the posterior interosseous artery
Formed by the median artery
questions.explanation: The deep palmar arch lies ~1 cm proximal to the superficial palmar arch directly across the bases of the metacarpals and interossei, supplied mainly by the radial artery.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: From which artery do the princeps pollicis artery (to the thumb) and radialis indicis artery (to the lateral index finger) arise?
options: Ulnar artery
Radial artery (as it enters the palm between the 1st dorsal interosseous and adductor pollicis)
Anterior interosseous artery
Superficial palmar arch
questions.explanation: Upon entering the palm, the radial artery gives off the princeps pollicis and radialis indicis arteries before continuing as the deep palmar arch.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which structure lies immediately LATERAL to the radial artery at the distal forearm (the classic site for palpating the radial pulse)?
options: Flexor carpi radialis tendon
Tendon of brachioradialis (and superficial branch of radial nerve in the middle third)
Palmaris longus tendon
Median nerve
questions.explanation: At the wrist, the radial pulse is palpated directly against the distal radius between the tendon of brachioradialis laterally and the tendon of flexor carpi radialis medially.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: What is the relationship between the ulnar artery and the ulnar nerve in the lower two-thirds of the forearm?
options: The ulnar nerve lies strictly MEDIAL to the ulnar artery
The ulnar nerve lies strictly LATERAL to the ulnar artery
The ulnar nerve winds spirally around the artery
They are separated by the interosseous membrane
questions.explanation: In the middle and lower thirds of the forearm, the ulnar artery is accompanied on its medial side by the ulnar nerve, both lying beneath flexor carpi ulnaris.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Why does infection in the synovial sheath of the little finger (ulnar bursa) or thumb (radial bursa) carry a high risk of spreading to the opposite digit or forearm?
options: Because the radial and ulnar bursae frequently communicate with each other deep to the flexor retinaculum and extend proximally into the space of Parona in the distal forearm (horseshoe abscess)
Because they drain directly into the cephalic vein
Because they pierce the interosseous membrane
Because they connect with the shoulder joint capsule
questions.explanation: The flexor tendon sheaths of the thumb (radial bursa) and little finger (ulnar bursa) extend through the carpal tunnel into the forearm and often intercommunicate, allowing 'horseshoe' spread of tenosynovitis.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which muscle is the ONLY muscle in the forearm or hand innervated by the radial nerve proximal to its bifurcation into superficial and deep branches (aside from brachioradialis and anconeus)?
options: Extensor carpi radialis longus
Extensor carpi radialis brevis
Extensor digitorum
Abductor pollicis longus
questions.explanation: Brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus arise from the lateral supracondylar ridge and are supplied by the main radial nerve trunk before it divides into superficial and deep (posterior interosseous) branches.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: Which test is performed before radial artery cannulation or harvesting (e.g., for coronary bypass) to confirm adequate collateral blood flow to the hand via the ulnar artery?
options: Trendelenburg test
Modified Allen's test
Phalen's test
Tinel's test
questions.explanation: The modified Allen's test occludes both radial and ulnar arteries while the patient clenches the fist, then releases the ulnar artery to verify rapid palmar flushing (<5–10 seconds) through the palmar arches.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: UL
questions.stem: A patient suffers a deep glass laceration on the volar aspect of the wrist just medial to the flexor carpi radialis tendon. Which nerve is most likely severed, and what is the primary functional deficit?
options: Ulnar nerve; loss of finger abduction/adduction
Median nerve; paralysis of thenar muscles (loss of thumb opposition—ape hand) and anesthesia of the palmar lateral 3½ digits
Radial nerve; wrist drop
Musculocutaneous nerve; loss of elbow flexion
questions.explanation: The median nerve lies immediately medial to the flexor carpi radialis tendon (and deep to palmaris longus) just proximal to the carpal tunnel; laceration here causes ape-hand deformity, loss of thumb opposition, and sensory loss over the lateral 3½ digits.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank
